evidence_quotes.quote: El resultado indica que el 23% de la población no dispone de una conexión de agua potable a través de la red pública, mientras que el 32% carece de un sistema de alcantarillado. En consecuencia, el 77% de la población cuenta con una conexión domiciliaria de agua potable y el 68% dispone de acceso a una red de alcantarillado.

Sin embargo, en las entrevistas a los funcionarios de la UESST, se tiene como resultado que, de la población que cuenta con conexión (77%), el 67.3% tiene conexión activa y el 32.7% no tiene conexión activa, por lo que en consecuencia solo el 51.8% cuenta con servicio efectivo de agua potable, con una continuidad de solo 2 horas diarias en promedio y en algunos sectores Inter diario.

el alto porcentaje de conexiones inactivas se debe al desabastecimiento del servicio en las zonas de la Localidad de Aguas Verdes y parte de Zarumilla, esto debido a las deficiencias que presenta actualmente la infraestructura de los sistemas de bombeo, almacenamiento y distribución ya sea por la antigüedad, deterioro y reparaciones que han sufrido, a la fecha no permite cubrir la demanda total del servicio ni mucho menos realizar mejoras en los niveles de presión y continuidad del servicio.

En el caso de la presente investigación, la población del distrito de Aguas Verdes, en la encuesta manifestó que el mal estado de los servicios de saneamiento y obras, se debe en parte a factores de corrupción de los funcionarios de las entidades públicas vinculadas a dichos servicios.

La SUNASS a pesar de contar con el marco normativo para ejecutar fiscalización anual, no evidencia que haya efectuado supervisión al 2021, ni que haya sancionado a la UESST por incumplimiento del Reglamento de Calidad de la Prestación de los Servicios de Saneamiento.

La información obtenida es el resultado de la encuesta tomada a una muestra de 94 pobladores del distrito de Aguas Verdes, realizada en el mes de junio del 2021; así como, entrevistas a funcionarios y revisión de documentación de la UESST, y del resultado del taller participativo de dirigentes comunales.

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household drinking-water and sanitation (sewerage) service access, active versus inactive utility connections, and supply continuity in the urban district of Aguas Verdes, Zarumilla province, Tumbes region, Peru.
criterion_notes.c2: PLAIN WORDING = YES; NARROW 2026-10-13 RULE-TYPE READING = NO (passes plain wording of Criterion 2 but fails narrow rule-type scope). Under the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the thesis examines institutional, administrative, and governance factors in urban sanitation delivery—specifically operational and civil-works management by UESST and the District Municipality of Aguas Verdes (MDAV), lack of citizen participation in civil-works proposals, municipal political interference, perceived corruption in public-works procurement, and a noted absence of SUNASS oversight/sanctions by 2021. Under the active 2026-10-13 clarification, however, Criterion 2 is restricted to rule-type mechanisms directly governing service access (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or analysed utility-ownership/regulatory rules directly governing access) rather than generic project delivery, behavioural promotion, or macro-governance background. Empirically, this Social Management thesis is a broad diagnostic of physical water-source scarcity (reliance on Pozo N° 6 in Zarumilla), 40-to-50-year-old deteriorated infrastructure causing 32.7% inactive connections, civil-works execution, lack of sanitary education, and general perceptions of procurement corruption. Tariffs are discussed only in abstract literature review (Section 4.1) and never studied empirically in Aguas Verdes; the 2005–2018 private concession vs. post-2018 OTASS/UESST regime is presented only as historical context (Section 3.3) without empirical comparison; and the single interview bullet noting no SUNASS supervision/sanctioning by 2021 is unanalysed institutional background rather than an analysis of a rule-type mechanism governing household access.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary mixed-methods empirical data collected in 2020–2021: a probabilistic cross-sectional survey of Aguas Verdes residents (calculated sample n = 94; most frequency tables report 95 respondents and Table 18 reports 73), semi-structured interviews with 11 officials (8 UESST, 1 MDAV, 2 ODS-Tumbes/SUNASS), institutional document review, and a February 2020 participatory workshop.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports relevant household and utility-level service access outcomes in Aguas Verdes: formal drinking-water network connection (77%), sewer network connection (68%), active vs. inactive water connections (67.3% active and 32.7% inactive among registered connections, yielding 51.8% effective water coverage), supply continuity (1–2 hours/day on average or inter-daily), and user satisfaction with supply frequency.
criterion_notes.c5: Provides sufficient detail to identify the population and unit of analysis (households/residents of Aguas Verdes district for the survey; utility/local institutions for key-informant interviews), the public-management and infrastructure factors examined (which fail C2's narrow rule-type scope), the service access outcomes, and the descriptive mixed-methods case-study design (despite minor reporting discrepancies such as n = 94 in sampling vs. n = 95 in most tables and narrative-only reporting of corruption survey responses in Section 5.4).
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in Spanish (with an English abstract on PDF Page 5). Although Spanish is not among the three languages eligible without translation (English, Portuguese, Dutch), the full text is completely readable and translation is directly feasible per Inclusion Criterion 10, so language does not bar assessment.

study_design: Mixed-methods descriptive case study (cross-sectional household survey, semi-structured key-informant interviews, document review, and participatory workshop)
population_and_sample: Households/residents of Aguas Verdes district, Zarumilla province, Tumbes region, Peru (sampling frame reported as 4,000 families / 16,000 inhabitants; probabilistic survey sample calculated as n = 94, with 95 responses reported in most tables), plus 11 semi-structured institutional interviews (8 UESST, 1 MDAV, 2 ODS-Tumbes/SUNASS) and participants in a February 2020 community-institutional workshop.
exposure: Generic public-sector operational management, civil-works project delivery, physical water-source scarcity and aging infrastructure, lack of citizen participation and sanitary education, political interference, unanalysed lack of routine regulatory supervision, and perceived corruption in public-works procurement (no rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing household service access).
outcome: Household drinking-water connection coverage (77%), sewer connection coverage (68%), active vs. inactive water connections (67.3% active, yielding 51.8% effective water service coverage), supply continuity (1 to 2 hours per day or inter-daily), user satisfaction, perceived sewer maintenance, and self-reported waterborne illness symptoms.
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) applying the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type scope of Criterion 2. This 2025 Peruvian Social Management master's thesis empirically documents household water and sewer coverage, active vs. inactive connections, and severe rationing (1–2 hours/day) in Aguas Verdes, Tumbes using a resident survey, official interviews, and a participatory workshop (satisfying c1, c3, c4, c5, and c6 via feasible Spanish translation). Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it would be included because it examines public management, citizen participation in public works, political interference, lack of SUNASS supervision, and perceived corruption in public-works contracting. Under the 2026-10-13 adjudication, however, it fails Criterion 2 because it does not empirically examine any rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing household access (such as eligibility screening, tenure/documentation requirements, administrative burden, tariff/disconnection rules, or analysed ownership/enforcement rules governing access); inactive connections and low coverage are attributed to physical water-source scarcity, deteriorated pumping/pipe infrastructure, generic project delivery deficits, and broad public-works corruption perceptions.
